fetched_contents.text: Thoughts, Attitudes and Experiences of Parents of Children with Disabilities in the Republic of North Macedonia About Comprehensive Sexuality Education Abstract When it comes to sexuality education, people with disabilities are often left out of the conversation. Many believe that these people are asexual, sexually inactive, that they do not need sexual education, that they cannot and should not have sexual relations and cannot/should not have love relationships and start a family. The main purpose of the research is to determinate thoughts, attitudes, knowledge and personal experience of the parents of children with disabilities regarding comprehensive sexuality education of their children. The data were collected through a survey of 54 respondents, parents of persons/children with disabilities from different regions in the Republic of N. Macedonia. Data were analyzed using the SPSS program and Chi square and Fisher exact test. From the data, it can be concluded that the majority of parents covered by this research are not familiar with the most appropriate age at which sexual education should begin. Around 57% of parents completely agreed with the statement that sex education should be part of the educational program in schools and only 38.9% of parents believe that their child should study all subjects. Children with disabilities need developmentally appropriate sex education to stay safe and healthy and to achieve self-determination. Keywords: Disabilities, Comprehensive sex education, Attitudes, Parents, North Macedonia Introduction In “The International Technical Guide to Sexuality Education” created by UNESCO, UNAIDS, UNFPA, UNICEF, UN WOMEN and WHO comprehensive sex education is defined as “a curriculum-based process of teaching and learning about the cognitive, emotional, physical and social aspects of sexuality. Aims to provide children and young people with knowledge, skills, attitudes and values that will encourage them to realize their health, well-being and dignity; to build social and sexual relationships based on respect; to consider how their choices affect their well-being and the well-being of others; and, to understand and ensure the defense of their rights throughout their lives” [1]. The International Planned Parenthood Federation points out that there is no single definition of comprehensive sex education and that they explain it as a holistic, developmentally and age appropriate, culturally and contextually relevant and scientifically accurate learning process, grounded in a vision of human rights, gender equality, positivism towards sex relationships that aim to: * Encourage children and young people to maintain their rights and the rights of others and to contribute to the achievement of an equal, diverse, compassionate and just society; * Enable children and young people to make decisions about their health and have access to key sexual and reproductive health services; * Increase the abilities of children and young people to engage in equal, happy, healthy, fulfilling and consensual relationships and experiences; [2]. All people are born as sexual beings and have to develop their sexual potential in some way. Sexuality education helps prepare young people for life, especially for building and maintaining fulfilling relationships, and contributes to their positive personal development and self-determination. The need for sex education has arisen due to several developmental stages in the last decade. This includes the rapid spread of new media, specifically the internet and mobile phones, the emergence and spread of HIV/AIDS, the growing concern about sexual abuse of children and adolescents, and changing attitudes towards sexuality and changing sexual behavior among young people. This calls for effective strategies to enable young people to deal with their sexuality in a safe and satisfying way [3]. Foremost, sexual education is a basic right of every person. The right to sexuality education is a universal human right, including the right to education and health, and is enshrined in numerous international agreements, such as the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the Convention on the Limination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, as well as the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Historically, people with disabilities have often been seen as asexual or sexually inactive, so sex education has generally been seen as unnecessary and even harmful for them. Already existing education for young people with disabilities often presents sex as dangerous and the sexuality of people with disabilities as problematic. Traditionally, the sexual life of people with disabilities was actively ignored and socially stigmatized. This topic was constantly ignored because it was considered a taboo topic. Additionally, sexuality as a form of pleasure and expression of love is still not recognized for people with disabilities. Also, some socio-cultural beliefs have contributed to barriers that prevent people with disabilities from exploring their sexuality [4]. All young people with disabilities are sexual beings and have the same right to enjoy their sexuality within the highest standards of health, including pleasurable and safe sexual experiences, free from coercion and violence, and to have access to quality sexuality education and services for sexual and reproductive health [1]. fetched_contents.text: Representations of Sexuality among Persons with Intellectual Disability, as Perceived by Professionals in Specialized Institutions: A Systematic Review Abstract The objective of this systematic review is to make an inventory of the representations of the professionals of specialized institutions on the sexuality of persons with intellectual disabilities. The scientific studies were identified according to the PRISMA protocol using 18 databases, with keywords on sexuality and parenthood. Studies were reviewed through a methodological assessment and then a thematic analysis. Twenty-four studies were reviewed and three themes were identified: professionals’ representations of gender, sexuality, and consent; professionals’ perceptions of their role in supporting people’s sexual lives; and the ways in which professionals construct representations of people’s sexual lives. This corpus highlights deep paradoxes in the representations of professionals concerning the socio-affective needs and sexuality of people with intellectual disabilities, creating what we could define as a “system of incompatibility” and leading to difficulties in positioning. Support is still too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, who are perceived as vulnerable. Training and new ways of teamwork appear to be central to supporting the evolution of the representations and practices of professionals. Future research anchored in practices and involving users as well as professionals is necessary to better understand the paradoxical aspects of professionals’ representations and to draw alternative ways of constructing these representations. Keywords: systematic review, intellectual disability, sexuality, mental representations, professionals, specialized institution 1. Introduction While the right to sexuality and an emotional life for individuals with intellectual disability is now widely recognized by global bodies such as the United Nations (The standard rules on the equalization of opportunities for persons with disabilities, 1994; United Nations, 2008) [1,2], its implementation remains seriously hampered. Many international studies—as well as a few studies undertaken in France—have focused on the measures that support the emotional and sex lives of such people and on the training that the professionals who care for them require. The international studies undertaken on the issue have given rise to a vast body of literature [3], ranging from instrumental approaches to sexuality to reflections that focus more on the love lives of people with an intellectual disability. These individuals have therefore been the subject of numerous studies on the potential obstacles to their sex lives and with regard to their social and emotional needs. However, practices on the ground have been slow to evolve [4]. Indeed, while researchers and practitioners have focused on the creation of programs that both professionals and these individuals themselves can use, there seems to be a paradox here [5,6]. This paradox is between professionals’ recognition of good practices concerning one’s sex and emotional life, which one can choose freely, and the functioning of the institutions that care for people with disabilities, which occasionally deny them their rights. In France, several researchers [7,8] have highlighted the existence of several preconceptions among professionals working in specialized institutions, including educators, carers, nurses, and psychologists. The sexuality of individuals with intellectual disabilities is still perceived negatively and in a very binary way. Indeed, it is seen either as non-existent among individuals viewed as asexual, or as bestial—a mere instinctive impulse [9,10,11]. This systematic review seeks to analyze the representations of professionals from specialized institutions (educators, carers, nurses, psychologists, executives, directors of structures) with regard to the sexuality of individuals with intellectual disabilities, and how these representations affect their perception of these individuals’ emotional lives. A better understanding of these representations may shed new light on how the sex lives of individuals with an intellectual disability (ID) may be supported, and thus promote the evolution of practices. How do these professionals perceive the sexuality of the people they support on a daily basis, and how do they perceive their role, especially with regard to the emotional and sex life projects of these individuals? 2. The objective of this project is to gain a better understanding of the specific needs and desires—in terms of the emotional, sexual, and parental lives of people with intellectual disabilities living in medical and social centers—in order to propose alternative support options for residents and innovative training for professionals. This research project was motivated by clinical questions arising from field observations: residents of medical and social centers hardly expressed their desire for an emotional life; even less did they express the desire to have children. fetched_contents.text: Sexual Self-Determination of Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities—A Possible Philosophical Conceptualization and Resulting Practical Challenges Abstract (1) Background: Self-determination is one of the central values of many societies. Self-determination concerns many areas of life, including sexuality. Unfortunately, the sexuality of individuals with intellectual disabilities (IID) is often discriminated against, and even in their everyday care, sexuality is often given too little space, not least because of knowledge deficits of parents and staff. Buck v. Parental attitudes toward sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities are shaped by strong protective instincts and a tendency to see sexuality as a risk rather than a normal, personal experience. The North Macedonia study explicitly notes that many parents believe people with disabilities are “asexual,” “sexually inactive,” “cannot and should not have sexual relations,” and “cannot/should not have love relationships and start a family” [N1-F1]. This directly supports the common belief that people with intellectual disabilities should be protected from sexual activity, not because of objective harm, but because their sexuality is often dismissed as inappropriate, dangerous, or socially unacceptable.

The same study also emphasizes that parents often lack familiarity with appropriate age ranges for sexuality education and that sex education is seen by some as unnecessary or harmful for people with disabilities [N1-F1]. This aligns with the observation that sexual expression is treated as inappropriate or dangerous: rather than viewing sexuality as a normal developmental process, parents are more likely to associate it with risk, ignorance, and the need for control [N1-F1]. The study further highlights that parents’ attitudes are closely tied to broader stigma, including the idea that people with disabilities should be excluded from the conversation around sexuality, which makes sexual expression seem socially deviant rather than a legitimate part of life [N1-F1].

On parenting attitudes shaping supervision, disclosure, or control, the evidence suggests a pattern of overprotection and limited autonomy. The North Macedonia study concludes that children with disabilities “need developmentally appropriate sex education to stay safe and healthy and to achieve self-determination” [N1-F1]. This implies that parental attitudes often translate into excessive supervision, secrecy, or withholding of information, because the parents’ protective instincts are interpreted as safeguards against harm. The study also notes that parents are often unprepared to educate their children about sexuality, which further supports the idea that supervision is shaped by a lack of knowledge and a conservative stance toward disclosure [N1-F1]. The broader conceptual background in the sexual self-determination literature reinforces this: people with intellectual disabilities are often overlooked in debates about self-determination, and their sexuality is given too little space in everyday care because of knowledge deficits among parents and staff [N4-F3]. In other words, parental attitudes do not merely reflect individual prejudice; they help create a caregiving environment in which sexuality is controlled, minimized, or hidden rather than supported.

Taken together, the evidence points to a restrictive parental mindset: sexuality is treated as a threat, disclosure is treated as optional or harmful, and parenting attitudes are used to justify supervision and control rather than autonomy and self-determination [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Professional staff attitudes toward sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities are marked by over-reliance on risk management and safety concerns, while autonomy and consent are frequently downplayed. The systematic review of professionals’ representations of sexuality among people with intellectual disabilities finds that professionals often construct sexuality in a negative or binary way, seeing it as either non-existent (“asexual”) or “bestial”—a mere instinctive impulse [N2-F2]. This directly supports the idea that staff over-rely on risk management or safety over autonomy: instead of treating sexuality as a normal, meaningful aspect of life, professionals frame it as something to be protected against or controlled because it is perceived as dangerous [N2-F2].

The same review also identifies a “system of incompatibility” in professionals’ representations, in which good practices and institutional realities collide. Professionals recognize the importance of supporting people’s sexual lives and emotional needs, but institutions often deny those rights because they are perceived as vulnerable [N2-F2]. This reflects a differential treatment of sexual rights versus other rights: sexual rights are framed as secondary to safety and control, while other rights may receive more legitimacy in institutional practice [N2-F2]. The review emphasizes that support is still too random and subject to control logics, and that training and new teamwork are central to changing these representations and practices [N2-F2]. This implies inconsistent practice patterns, because staff are not uniformly equipped to support sexual rights in a way that aligns with autonomy.

The broader conceptual context in the sexual self-determination literature further explains this pattern. People with intellectual disabilities are often overlooked in debates about sexual self-determination, and their sexuality is given too little space in everyday care because of knowledge deficits among parents and staff [N4-F3]. This reinforces the idea that professionals’ attitudes are shaped by ignorance and stigma, which in turn lead to practices that prioritize risk reduction over genuine consent and self-determination [N4-F3]. The review also notes that professionals’ representations can create “paradoxes” between recognition of good practices and institutional denial of rights, which means staff may want to support sexual autonomy but still end up enforcing control [N2-F2].

In short, the evidence shows staff attitudes that are overly safety-focused, inconsistent in practice, and often discriminatory in how they treat sexual rights compared with other rights [N2-F2][N4-F3]. This contributes to a system in which sexuality is managed rather than respected, and where autonomy and consent are not the default assumptions of care [N2-F2].

Legal and custody-related constraints on parenting rights and decision-making for people with intellectual disabilities are substantial and often discriminatory. The most direct evidence is that people with intellectual disabilities face proceedings to terminate their parental rights with “disturbing regularity,” and the primary justification given is the protection of offspring’s interests [N5-F4]. This supports the claim that legal mechanisms are used to limit or terminate parental rights, often on the basis of disability rather than actual harm [N5-F4]. The article also points out that these termination proceedings involve problematic assumptions about how fitness to parent is understood and how parenting is legally constructed [N5-F4]. In other words, the law is not simply neutral; it often treats disability as a proxy for unfit parenting, even when there is no clear causal link between the disability and the child’s welfare [N5-F4].

Custody, guardianship, and supported decision-making frameworks are presented as alternative legal structures. The article argues that supported decision-making (SDM) and limited terminations analogous to limited guardianships are better models than the “all-or-nothing” termination process [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that supported decision-making allows individuals with disabilities to make choices about their own lives with support from a team they choose [N5-R2]. This directly supports the point that custody and guardianship frameworks can constrain autonomy, but they can also be restructured to protect decision-making rights [N5-R2][N5-F4]. The legal literature also highlights that custody, visitation, and access should not be denied or restricted because of a parent’s disability, and that there should be a showing that the disability is causally related to harm that cannot be alleviated with services, supports, or reasonable modifications [N5-F4]. This is important because it shows how law and policy can constrain autonomy and consent when disability is used as a proxy for decision-making capacity, rather than through a fair process of support and evidence [N5-F4].

The broader policy context in the parental rights literature also shows that disability is used as a statutory ground for termination of parental rights in many states, and that this can be challenged through antidiscrimination principles [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. The National Council on Disability and the American Bar Association have both called for protections that prevent disability from being treated as a reason to remove custody or terminate rights without sufficient evidence of harm [N5-F4]. This reinforces the claim that legal and policy frameworks often constrain autonomy and consent by making disability a legal barrier to parenting, rather than a disability-specific need for support [N5-F4][N6-R3].

Overall, the evidence shows a legal system that is both restrictive and discriminatory in its treatment of parenting rights. Legal mechanisms can be used to limit or terminate rights, custody and guardianship frameworks can shape decision-making, and supported decision-making offers a more rights-respecting alternative, but only if implemented fairly rather than as a substitute for real autonomy [N5-F4][N5-R2][N6-R3].

Restrictive practices and interventions affecting sexual rights and parenting have been observed in multiple ways, including physical, institutional, surveillance-based restrictions, separation from partners or sexual relationships, and overuse of interventions for perceived sexual risk.

First, physical and institutional restrictions are evident in the evidence base. The CQL research notes that discriminatory practices, biases, and ableist perceptions of people with intellectual disabilities affect parenting and sexual health rights, implying that institutional settings often impose barriers rather than support autonomy [N3-R3]. The disability rights chapter also states that when parents—including those with intellectual disabilities—are unable to provide for their children’s needs, their right to retain custody may be challenged, which can translate into institutional interventions that remove or limit parenting rights [N3-R4]. This supports the idea that custody and support decisions can be used as mechanisms of control rather than support [N3-R4].

Surveillance-based or control-oriented restrictions are also present. The earlier reports on professional staff attitudes show that support is too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, who are perceived as vulnerable [N2-F2]. That same review also describes a “system of incompatibility” in professionals’ representations, in which good practices are recognized but institutional realities deny rights because people are seen as vulnerable [N2-F2]. This pattern suggests that care environments may rely on monitoring, supervision, and institutional control rather than genuine autonomy and consent [N2-F2].

Separation from partners or sexual relationships is another observed restrictive practice. The CQL research explicitly identifies discriminatory practices that affect parenting and sexual health rights, including ableist perceptions that people with intellectual disabilities are incapable of parenting or engaging in sexual relationships [N3-R3]. The broader parental-attitudes evidence also shows that many parents believe people with disabilities “cannot and should not have sexual relations” and “cannot/should not have love relationships and start a family” [N1-F1]. Combined with the professional-staff evidence that sexuality is often framed as non-existent, bestial, or dangerous [N2-F2], this creates an environment in which people may be separated from partners or sexual relationships as a form of control [N3-R3][N1-F1][N2-F2].

Finally, restrictive interventions are overused for perceived sexual risk. The CQL research notes that discriminatory practices and ableist perceptions are used to limit parenting and sexual health rights, which suggests that interventions are often justified by fears of sexual risk rather than evidence of actual harm [N3-R3]. The earlier professional-staff report also shows that professionals may prioritize risk management or safety over autonomy, and that support is still too random and subject to control logics [N2-F2]. This means that people may be subjected to unnecessary restrictions, surveillance, or interventions simply because they are assumed to be at risk sexually, rather than because there is a justified and proportionate need for intervention [N2-F2][N3-R3].

Overall, the evidence points to a pattern of restrictive practices that include institutional control, surveillance, separation from relationships, and overuse of interventions for perceived sexual risk [N3-R3][N3-R4][N2-F2][N1-F1]. These practices are not isolated; they are shaped by both caregiving attitudes and institutional structures that prioritize protection and control over autonomy and consent [N2-F2][N3-R3].

Historical stigma and eugenic-era influences remain deeply embedded in the evidence. The sexual self-determination literature notes that people with intellectual disabilities have long been stigmatized as not sexual beings at all, and that this historical stigma continues to shape how sexuality is understood and managed [N4-F3]. The same source describes a long history in which people with disabilities were not considered sexual beings and were sometimes seen as morally responsible for their disabilities [N4-F3]. The legal and custody literature also shows that eugenic-era ideas continue to inform the treatment of parental rights, including the idea that people with intellectual disabilities may be unfit to parent because of disability rather than because of actual harm [N5-F4]. This historical stigma helps explain why sexual rights and parenting rights are still treated as exceptional, dangerous, or inappropriate [N4-F3][N5-F4].

Legal and policy constraints on autonomy and consent are another major reason these attitudes persist. The legal article on parental rights explains that people with intellectual disabilities face proceedings to terminate their parental rights with disturbing regularity, and that the law often uses disability as a proxy for unfit parenting rather than requiring evidence of actual harm [N5-F4]. It also argues that supported decision-making and limited terminations are better models than all-or-nothing termination processes, because current legal frameworks can constrain autonomy and consent by making disability a legal barrier to parenting [N5-F4][N5-R2]. This legal structure reinforces restrictive attitudes by treating disability as a legal disability rather than a need for support [N5-F4].

The evidence shows that restrictive attitudes toward the sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities are widespread and persistent. These attitudes are not limited to individual prejudice; they are shaped by broader caregiving norms, institutional structures, legal frameworks, and historical stigma. Across parents and professional staff, the dominant pattern is one of overprotection, risk management, and control, with sexuality and parenting often treated as exceptional, dangerous, or inappropriate rather than as legitimate and normal rights.

### 1. Parental attitudes: protection, secrecy, and control

Parents often treat people with intellectual disabilities as needing protection from sexual activity, rather than as people with a normal sexual life. The evidence from the North Macedonia study notes that many parents believe people with disabilities are “asexual,” “sexually inactive,” “cannot and should not have sexual relations,” and “cannot/should not have love relationships and start a family” [N1-F1]. The same study concludes that children with disabilities “need developmentally appropriate sex education to stay safe and healthy and to achieve self-determination” [N1-F1]. In other words, parental attitudes do not merely reflect individual prejudice; they help create a caregiving environment in which sexuality is controlled, minimized, or hidden rather than supported [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The systematic review of professionals’ representations of sexuality among people with intellectual disabilities finds that professionals often construct sexuality in a negative or binary way, seeing it as either non-existent (“asexual”) or “bestial”—a mere instinctive impulse [N2-F2]. ### 3. Observed restrictive practices and interventions in practice

The restrictive attitudes do not remain abstract; they are reflected in actual practices and interventions. These restrictive attitudes persist because of historical stigma, legal and policy constraints, and resource limitations and staff workload pressures.

### 6. Conclusion

Overall, the evidence points to a consistent pattern of restrictive attitudes toward the sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities. Parents often treat sexuality as a risk and use supervision, secrecy, and control to limit expression; professional staff often prioritize risk management over autonomy and may reinforce differential treatment of sexual rights; and institutional and legal systems often use disability as a barrier to parenting rights rather than as a need for support [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R3][N5-F4]. These attitudes are not simply prejudice; they are sustained by historical stigma, legal and policy constraints, and practical pressures that make control easier than support [N4-F3][N5-F4][N2-F2]. The result is a system in which sexual rights and parenting rights are too often treated as exceptional rather than as fundamental human rights [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

## Integrated final answer on restrictive attitudes toward sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities

The evidence shows that restrictive attitudes toward the sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities are widespread and persistent. These attitudes are not limited to individual prejudice; they are shaped by broader caregiving norms, institutional structures, legal frameworks, and historical stigma. Across parents and professional staff, the dominant pattern is one of overprotection, risk management, and control, with sexuality and parenting often treated as exceptional, dangerous, or inappropriate rather than as legitimate and normal rights.

### 1. Parental attitudes: protection, secrecy, and control

Parents often treat people with intellectual disabilities as needing protection from sexual activity, rather than as people with a normal sexual life. The evidence from the North Macedonia study notes that many parents believe people with disabilities are “asexual,” “sexually inactive,” “cannot and should not have sexual relations,” and “cannot/should not have love relationships and start a family” [N1-F1]. This directly supports the common belief that people with intellectual disabilities should be protected from sexual activity. It also shows that sexual expression is often treated as inappropriate or dangerous, rather than as a natural and legitimate part of life [N1-F1].

This mindset shapes supervision, disclosure, and control. The same study concludes that children with disabilities “need developmentally appropriate sex education to stay safe and healthy and to achieve self-determination” [N1-F1]. But the evidence suggests that parental attitudes often translate into excessive supervision, secrecy, and withholding of information. Parents may be unprepared to educate their children about sexuality, and the broader conceptual literature notes that people with intellectual disabilities are often overlooked in debates about self-determination, with their sexuality given too little space in everyday care because of knowledge deficits among parents and staff [N4-F3]. In other words, parental attitudes do not merely reflect individual prejudice; they help create a caregiving environment in which sexuality is controlled, minimized, or hidden rather than supported [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### 2. Professional staff attitudes: risk management over autonomy

Professional staff attitudes are similarly restrictive, but they are often more institutionalized. The systematic review of professionals’ representations of sexuality among people with intellectual disabilities finds that professionals often construct sexuality in a negative or binary way, seeing it as either non-existent (“asexual”) or “bestial”—a mere instinctive impulse [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that staff over-rely on risk management or safety concerns over autonomy. Instead of treating sexuality as a normal part of life, professionals frame it as something to be protected against or controlled because it is perceived as dangerous [N2-F2].

The same review identifies a “system of incompatibility” in professionals’ representations: professionals recognize the importance of supporting people’s sexual lives and emotional needs, but institutions often deny those rights because they are perceived as vulnerable [N2-F2]. This creates a differential treatment of sexual rights versus other rights: sexual rights are framed as secondary to safety and control, while other rights may receive more legitimacy in institutional practice [N2-F2]. The review also notes that support is still too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, and that training and new teamwork are central to changing these representations and practices [N2-F2]. This implies inconsistent practice patterns, because staff are not uniformly equipped to support sexual rights in a way that aligns with autonomy [N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 3. Observed restrictive practices and interventions in practice

The restrictive attitudes do not remain abstract; they are reflected in actual practices and interventions. The evidence shows that restrictive practices include physical, institutional, or surveillance-based restrictions. The CQL research notes that discriminatory practices, biases, and ableist perceptions of people with intellectual disabilities affect parenting and sexual health rights, implying that institutional settings often impose barriers rather than support autonomy [N3-R3]. The disability rights chapter also states that when parents—including those with intellectual disabilities—are unable to provide for their children’s needs, their right to retain custody may be challenged, which can translate into institutional interventions that remove or limit parenting rights [N3-R4].

Surveillance-based or control-oriented restrictions are also present. The earlier reports on professional staff attitudes show that support is too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, who are perceived as vulnerable [N2-F2]. That same review describes a “system of incompatibility” in professionals’ representations, in which good practices are recognized but institutional realities deny rights because people are seen as vulnerable [N2-F2]. This pattern suggests that care environments may rely on monitoring, supervision, and institutional control rather than genuine autonomy and consent [N2-F2].

Separation from partners or sexual relationships is another observed restrictive practice. The CQL research explicitly identifies discriminatory practices that affect parenting and sexual health rights, including ableist perceptions that people with intellectual disabilities are incapable of parenting or engaging in sexual relationships [N3-R3]. The parental-attitudes evidence also shows that many parents believe people with disabilities “cannot and should not have sexual relations” and “cannot/should not have love relationships and start a family” [N1-F1]. Combined with the professional-staff evidence that sexuality is often framed as non-existent, bestial, or dangerous [N2-F2], this creates an environment in which people may be separated from partners or sexual relationships as a form of control [N3-R3][N1-F1][N2-F2].

Finally, restrictive interventions are overused for perceived sexual risk. The CQL research notes that discriminatory practices and ableist perceptions are used to limit parenting and sexual health rights, which suggests that interventions are often justified by fears of sexual risk rather than evidence of actual harm [N3-R3]. The earlier professional-staff report also shows that professionals may prioritize risk management or safety over autonomy, and that support is still too random and subject to control logics [N2-F2]. This means that people may be subjected to unnecessary restrictions, surveillance, or interventions simply because they are assumed to be at risk sexually, rather than because there is a justified and proportionate need for intervention [N2-F2][N3-R3].

### 4. Legal and custody-related constraints

Legal and custody-related constraints are a major reason these attitudes persist. The legal evidence shows that people with intellectual disabilities face proceedings to terminate their parental rights with disturbing regularity, and that the primary justification is the protection of offspring’s interests [N5-F4]. This supports the claim that legal mechanisms are used to limit or terminate parental rights, often on the basis of disability rather than actual harm [N5-F4]. The article also points out that these termination proceedings involve problematic assumptions about how fitness to parent is understood and how parenting is legally constructed [N5-F4]. In other words, the law is not simply neutral; it often treats disability as a proxy for unfit parenting, even when there is no clear causal link between the disability and the child’s welfare [N5-F4].

Custody, guardianship, and supported decision-making frameworks are presented as alternative legal structures. The article argues that supported decision-making (SDM) and limited terminations analogous to limited guardianships are better models than the “all-or-nothing” termination process [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that supported decision-making allows individuals with disabilities to make choices about their own lives with support from a team they choose [N5-R2]. This directly supports the point that custody and guardianship frameworks can constrain autonomy, but they can also be restructured to protect decision-making rights [N5-R2][N5-F4]. The legal literature also highlights that custody, visitation, and access should not be denied or restricted because of a parent’s disability, and that there should be a showing that the disability is causally related to harm that cannot be alleviated with services, supports, or reasonable modifications [N5-F4]. This is important because it shows how law and policy can constrain autonomy and consent when disability is used as a proxy for decision-making capacity, rather than through a fair process of support and evidence [N5-F4].

The custody and legal-status evidence also shows that disability is used as a statutory ground for termination of parental rights in many states, and that this can be challenged through antidiscrimination principles [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. The National Council on Disability and the American Bar Association have both called for protections that prevent disability from being treated as a reason to remove custody or terminate rights without sufficient evidence of harm [N5-F4]. This reinforces the claim that legal and policy frameworks often constrain autonomy and consent by making disability a legal barrier to parenting, rather than a disability-specific need for support [N5-F4][N6-R3].

### 5. Broader context and why these attitudes persist

These restrictive attitudes persist because of historical stigma, legal and policy constraints, and resource limitations and staff workload pressures.

**Historical stigma and eugenic-era influences remain deeply embedded.** The sexual self-determination literature notes that people with intellectual disabilities have long been stigmatized as not sexual beings at all, and that this historical stigma continues to shape how sexuality is understood and managed [N4-F3]. The same source describes a long history in which people with disabilities were not considered sexual beings and were sometimes seen as morally responsible for their disabilities [N4-F3]. The legal and custody literature also shows that eugenic-era ideas continue to inform the treatment of parental rights, including the idea that people with intellectual disabilities may be unfit to parent because of disability rather than because of actual harm [N5-F4]. This historical stigma helps explain why sexual rights and parenting rights are still treated as exceptional, dangerous, or inappropriate [N4-F3][N5-F4].

**Legal and policy constraints on autonomy and consent are another major reason.** The legal article on parental rights explains that people with intellectual disabilities face proceedings to terminate their parental rights with disturbing regularity, and that the law often uses disability as a proxy for unfit parenting rather than requiring evidence of actual harm [N5-F4]. It also argues that supported decision-making and limited terminations are better models than all-or-nothing termination processes, because current legal frameworks can constrain autonomy and consent by making disability a legal barrier to parenting [N5-F4][N5-R2]. The custody and guardianship evidence similarly shows that custody, visitation, and access should not be denied or restricted because of disability, and that there must be a showing that the disability is causally related to harm that cannot be alleviated with services or reasonable modifications [N5-F4]. This legal structure reinforces restrictive attitudes by treating disability as a legal disability rather than a need for support [N5-F4].

**Resource limitations and staff workload pressures further sustain restrictive attitudes.** The professional-staff evidence shows that support is still too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, and that training and new teamwork are central to changing representations and practices [N2-F2]. The broader conceptual evidence also notes that knowledge deficits among parents and staff contribute to the underestimation of sexual self-determination and the overemphasis on control [N4-F3]. These pressures create an environment in which staff may rely on risk management, surveillance, and control rather than on autonomy-supporting practices, because they lack training and are burdened by workload [N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 6. Conclusion

Overall, the evidence points to a consistent pattern of restrictive attitudes toward the sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities. Parents often treat sexuality as a risk and use supervision, secrecy, and control to limit expression; professional staff often prioritize risk management over autonomy and may reinforce differential treatment of sexual rights; and institutional and legal systems often use disability as a barrier to parenting rights rather than as a need for support [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R3][N5-F4]. These attitudes are not simply prejudice; they are sustained by historical stigma, legal and policy constraints, and practical pressures that make control easier than support [N4-F3][N5-F4][N2-F2]. The result is a system in which sexual rights and parenting rights are too often treated as exceptional rather than as fundamental human rights [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

In other words, parental attitudes do not merely reflect individual prejudice; they help create a caregiving environment in which sexuality is controlled, minimized, or hidden rather than supported [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### 2. Professional staff attitudes: risk management over autonomy

Professional staff attitudes are similarly restrictive, but they are often more institutionalized. The systematic review of professionals’ representations of sexuality among people with intellectual disabilities finds that professionals often construct sexuality in a negative or binary way, seeing it as either non-existent (“asexual”) or “bestial”—a mere instinctive impulse [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that staff over-rely on risk management or safety concerns over autonomy. Instead of treating sexuality as a normal part of life, professionals frame it as something to be protected against or controlled because it is perceived as dangerous [N2-F2].

The same review identifies a “system of incompatibility” in professionals’ representations: professionals recognize the importance of supporting people’s sexual lives and emotional needs, but institutions often deny those rights because they are perceived as vulnerable [N2-F2]. This creates a differential treatment of sexual rights versus other rights: sexual rights are framed as secondary to safety and control, while other rights may receive more legitimacy in institutional practice [N2-F2]. The review also notes that support is still too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, and that training and new teamwork are central to changing these representations and practices [N2-F2]. This implies inconsistent practice patterns, because staff are not uniformly equipped to support sexual rights in a way that aligns with autonomy [N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 3. Observed restrictive practices and interventions in practice

The restrictive attitudes do not remain abstract; they are reflected in actual practices and interventions. The evidence shows that restrictive practices include physical, institutional, or surveillance-based restrictions. The CQL research notes that discriminatory practices, biases, and ableist perceptions of people with intellectual disabilities affect parenting and sexual health rights, implying that institutional settings often impose barriers rather than support autonomy [N3-R3]. The disability rights chapter also states that when parents—including those with intellectual disabilities—are unable to provide for their children’s needs, their right to retain custody may be challenged, which can translate into institutional interventions that remove or limit parenting rights [N3-R4].

Surveillance-based or control-oriented restrictions are also present. The earlier reports on professional staff attitudes show that support is too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, who are perceived as vulnerable [N2-F2]. That same review describes a “system of incompatibility” in professionals’ representations, in which good practices are recognized but institutional realities deny rights because people are seen as vulnerable [N2-F2]. This pattern suggests that care environments may rely on monitoring, supervision, and institutional control rather than genuine autonomy and consent [N2-F2].

Separation from partners or sexual relationships is another observed restrictive practice. The CQL research explicitly identifies discriminatory practices that affect parenting and sexual health rights, including ableist perceptions that people with intellectual disabilities are incapable of parenting or engaging in sexual relationships [N3-R3]. The parental-attitudes evidence also shows that many parents believe people with disabilities “cannot and should not have sexual relations” and “cannot/should not have love relationships and start a family” [N1-F1]. Combined with the professional-staff evidence that sexuality is often framed as non-existent, bestial, or dangerous [N2-F2], this creates an environment in which people may be separated from partners or sexual relationships as a form of control [N3-R3][N1-F1][N2-F2].

Finally, restrictive interventions are overused for perceived sexual risk. The CQL research notes that discriminatory practices and ableist perceptions are used to limit parenting and sexual health rights, which suggests that interventions are often justified by fears of sexual risk rather than evidence of actual harm [N3-R3]. The earlier professional-staff report also shows that professionals may prioritize risk management or safety over autonomy, and that support is still too random and subject to control logics [N2-F2]. This means that people may be subjected to unnecessary restrictions, surveillance, or interventions simply because they are assumed to be at risk sexually, rather than because there is a justified and proportionate need for intervention [N2-F2][N3-R3].

### 4. Legal and custody-related constraints

Legal and custody-related constraints are a major reason these attitudes persist. The legal evidence shows that people with intellectual disabilities face proceedings to terminate their parental rights with disturbing regularity, and that the primary justification is the protection of offspring’s interests [N5-F4]. This supports the claim that legal mechanisms are used to limit or terminate parental rights, often on the basis of disability rather than actual harm [N5-F4]. The article also points out that these termination proceedings involve problematic assumptions about how fitness to parent is understood and how parenting is legally constructed [N5-F4]. In other words, the law is not simply neutral; it often treats disability as a proxy for unfit parenting, even when there is no clear causal link between the disability and the child’s welfare [N5-F4].

Custody, guardianship, and supported decision-making frameworks are presented as alternative legal structures. The article argues that supported decision-making (SDM) and limited terminations analogous to limited guardianships are better models than the “all-or-nothing” termination process [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that supported decision-making allows individuals with disabilities to make choices about their own lives with support from a team they choose [N5-R2]. This directly supports the point that custody and guardianship frameworks can constrain autonomy, but they can also be restructured to protect decision-making rights [N5-R2][N5-F4]. The legal literature also highlights that custody, visitation, and access should not be denied or restricted because of a parent’s disability, and that there should be a showing that the disability is causally related to harm that cannot be alleviated with services, supports, or reasonable modifications [N5-F4]. This is important because it shows how law and policy can constrain autonomy and consent when disability is used as a proxy for decision-making capacity, rather than through a fair process of support and evidence [N5-F4].

The custody and legal-status evidence also shows that disability is used as a statutory ground for termination of parental rights in many states, and that this can be challenged through antidiscrimination principles [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. The National Council on Disability and the American Bar Association have both called for protections that prevent disability from being treated as a reason to remove custody or terminate rights without sufficient evidence of harm [N5-F4]. This reinforces the claim that legal and policy frameworks often constrain autonomy and consent by making disability a legal barrier to parenting, rather than a disability-specific need for support [N5-F4][N6-R3].

### 5. Broader context and why these attitudes persist

These restrictive attitudes persist because of historical stigma, legal and policy constraints, and resource limitations and staff workload pressures.

**Historical stigma and eugenic-era influences remain deeply embedded.** The sexual self-determination literature notes that people with intellectual disabilities have long been stigmatized as not sexual beings at all, and that this historical stigma continues to shape how sexuality is understood and managed [N4-F3]. The same source describes a long history in which people with disabilities were not considered sexual beings and were sometimes seen as morally responsible for their disabilities [N4-F3]. The legal and custody literature also shows that eugenic-era ideas continue to inform the treatment of parental rights, including the idea that people with intellectual disabilities may be unfit to parent because of disability rather than because of actual harm [N5-F4]. This historical stigma helps explain why sexual rights and parenting rights are still treated as exceptional, dangerous, or inappropriate [N4-F3][N5-F4].

**Legal and policy constraints on autonomy and consent are another major reason.** The legal article on parental rights explains that people with intellectual disabilities face proceedings to terminate their parental rights with disturbing regularity, and that the law often uses disability as a proxy for unfit parenting rather than requiring evidence of actual harm [N5-F4]. It also argues that supported decision-making and limited terminations are better models than all-or-nothing termination processes, because current legal frameworks can constrain autonomy and consent by making disability a legal barrier to parenting [N5-F4][N5-R2]. The custody and guardianship evidence similarly shows that custody, visitation, and access should not be denied or restricted because of disability, and that there must be a showing that the disability is causally related to harm that cannot be alleviated with services or reasonable modifications [N5-F4]. This legal structure reinforces restrictive attitudes by treating disability as a legal disability rather than a need for support [N5-F4].

**Resource limitations and staff workload pressures further sustain restrictive attitudes.** The professional-staff evidence shows that support is still too random and subject to control logics in the name of protecting users, and that training and new teamwork are central to changing representations and practices [N2-F2]. The broader conceptual evidence also notes that knowledge deficits among parents and staff contribute to the underestimation of sexual self-determination and the overemphasis on control [N4-F3]. These pressures create an environment in which staff may rely on risk management, surveillance, and control rather than on autonomy-supporting practices, because they lack training and are burdened by workload [N2-F2][N4-F3].

### 6. Conclusion

Overall, the evidence points to a consistent pattern of restrictive attitudes toward the sexual rights and parenting of people with intellectual disabilities. Parents often treat sexuality as a risk and use supervision, secrecy, and control to limit expression; professional staff often prioritize risk management over autonomy and may reinforce differential treatment of sexual rights; and institutional and legal systems often use disability as a barrier to parenting rights rather than as a need for support [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R3][N5-F4]. These attitudes are not simply prejudice; they are sustained by historical stigma, legal and policy constraints, and practical pressures that make control easier than support [N4-F3][N5-F4][N2-F2]. The result is a system in which sexual rights and parenting rights are too often treated as exceptional rather than as fundamental human rights [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].
